utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, Belinda Pidwell, Joanna Korner, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. We have quite an international Defence team today for Mr. Slobodan [as interpreted] Stanisic. Attorney-at-law, Slobodan Zecevic, Republika Srpska; Deirdre Montgomery, Ireland; and for the first time Ivana Batista from the Netherlands; and of course Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and our learned friend, solicitor from London, originally from Denmark, Mr. Lennart Poulsen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. For the record, Slobodan Cvijetic, Republika Srpska; Eugene O'Sullivan, Canada; Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, Ireland; and Ms. Ivana Batista, the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript would -- records Ms. Montgomery as being from "Island." Of course, it's Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "Ireland," that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a preliminary matter we'd like to raise before the witness is brought in, and it refers -- relates to the 92 ter package that the Prosecution is offering with the next witness. And it's our submission we should deal with this outside the presence of the witness, as we anticipate that he'll comply with the 92 ter formalities, and it's on the admission of the supporting materials to the package and certain aspects of his statement that we take objection to. The 92 ter package includes 15 newspaper articles that were written by the witness. Let me begin by saying that we take -- we have a standing objection to the admissibility of newspaper articles, which I would reiterate here. These articles, as Your Honours may have seen, contain a large amount of unverified and, in fact, unverifiable information from local radios, Radio Sarajevo, the Tanjug News Agency, Croatian Radio, accounts that the witness claims he heard on those news sources. He attributes words to persons who are often named or at times unnamed. It contains accounts of information from unnamed foreign officials, Western observers, and local politicians. And in particular in relation to one article, which is at tab 7, 65 ter 3377, we say the article is wholly irrelevant. It relates to the Sarajevo air-lift, an article published in July. It has nothing to do with our indictment. That's the first general objection. The second objection has to do with interviews that were conducted by Mr. Traynor, and I refer you to tab 2, 65 ter 10358.02. That's Mr. Traynor's OTP interview. And at page 7, he says: "During this time, I also carried out interviews of survivors of the three main detention facilities which existed in the Prijedor area. My investigations are outlined in articles that I wrote on the subject." And we find, similarly, at tab 14, 65 ter 3373, his article on the 6th of October, 1992, on page 1, where he states that: "Since last week, 'The Guardian' has conducted lengthy detailed and separate interviews with many of the former inmates and their relatives." Now, the articles I'm referring to are contained at tabs 12 through 17 inclusive. They're the articles that date from the 2nd of October and later. Your Honour, we say, as a matter of law, this information is not admissible through Traynor, and we refer you to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in the Milutinovic case, IT-05-87-T, a decision of the 1st of September, 2006. It's a decision on the evidence tendered through Sandra Mitchell and Frederick Abrams. And, similarly, on the 8th of September, 2006, a decision on evidence tendered through Fuad Haxhibeqiri. We say that this jurisprudence applies to this context of what is being offered through Mr. Traynor, and I'll explain why. The facts of the case of the decisions in Milutinovic were the following: International organisations had prepared reports, and these reports were not prepared for the purpose of litigation. We say the same applies to the articles written by Mr. Traynor. They were not prepared for the purposes of litigation. The reports in Milutinovic that were prepared by the NGOs contained excerpts of statements of alleged criminal conduct that were made by persons who claimed to be the victims of or witnesses to crimes. The statements were taken by people from the NGOs who did not participate in the events and did not see or experience the events or the accounts that were described by the declarants. They were NGO people who met with people who claimed to be victims. And the same is true here. Mr. Traynor, in October, claims to have interviewed people who were in these facilities. The Milutinovic Trial Chamber, in the two decisions I've cited, found that these accounts were inadmissible hearsay, and the reasoning of the Milutinovic Chamber followed the Appeals Chamber decision in Aleksovski. That's case IT-95-14/1-AR73, 16 February 1999. It's the decision on the Prosecutor's appeal on admissibility of evidence. And at paragraph 44 of that decision, the Appeals Chamber discusses the issue of the indicia of reliability and the admission of summary hearsay evidence. And two points flow from that Appeals Chamber decision which were followed in Milutinovic. The first matter is this: A Chamber must consider whether the summary is first-hand hearsay, and by that the Appeals Chamber said the issue is whether the person who made the summary personally saw or heard the events recorded in the statement. The second point is that -- is whether the absence of opportunity to cross-examine those persons, the declarant, affects the statement. And the third point made by the Appeals Chamber is that the opportunity to simply be able to cross-examine the person who summarised the statement, the person who recorded what was told, does not overcome the absence of opportunity to cross-examine the declarant. The situation with Mr. Traynor is identical to the situation in Milutinovic. Mr. Traynor wrote things he was told by others and published them in the newspaper. Mr. Traynor neither saw nor heard the events that were recorded, and we have no opportunity to cross-examine the declarants. You, as the Trial Chamber, do not have sufficient indicia or material to be satisfied that the information contained in Mr. Traynor's articles is reliable. There is an avenue for the Prosecution to have the statements of declarants heard by you, and that is by calling the witness viva voce or by using 92 ter or 92 bis. They are inadmissible through the 92 ter package and the newspaper articles tendered -- attempted to be tendered through Mr. Traynor. We say the same is true for certain aspects of Mr. Traynor's OTP interview, which is 65 ter 10358.2. There, at page 8, he has an interview with a man named Krzic, on page 8 with a man named Sadic, from pages 13 to 16 he has discussions or conversations -- general conversations with Mr. Karadzic, Koljevic, Veljko Ostojic, Ratko Mladic, Mr. Milanovic, and a Colonel Milutinovic, some of which are outside the scope of the indictment. Again, Mr. Traynor neither saw or heard the events that these people are discussing, and we have no opportunity to cross-examine the declarant. The last objection we have relates to what we anticipate Mr. Traynor giving an account -- a hearsay account of what was told to him by ICRC employees. Again, I refer you to tab 2 of 65 ter 10358.2, which is Mr. Traynor's OTP interview. At page 2, he says: "Another person I interviewed who gave a good background to account of what happened in Banja Luka was an international humanitarian official who was the only international person in Banja Luka and Northern Bosnia." He explains in the proofing note of 7 April that it is an ICRC employee. Four of his newspaper articles make reference to accounts given by an ICRC employee. That's tab 9, 65 ter 3376 at page 2; tab 10, 65 ter 3375 at page 2; tab 13, 65 ter 10358 .07 at pages 1 and 2; and, finally, at tab 16, 65 ter 10058.08 at page 2. Now, why do we say that the statements or information provided by an ICRC employee are inadmissible? I direct Your Honours to the decision in the Prosecutor versus Simic, IT-95-9-PT, a decision dated 27 July 1999. It's a decision on the Prosecution motion under Rule 73 for a ruling concerning the testimony of a witness. The witness in question was a former ICRC employee. The Chamber found that an employee or former employee of the ICRC cannot testify before the ICTY. The Chamber found that there is a rule of customary international law which bars the admission of evidence given by an ICRC employee. The Chamber held that the ratification of the Geneva Conventions by 188 states can be considered as reflecting the opinio juris of these states, which, in addition to the general practice of states in relation to the ICRC, leaves the Chamber to conclude that the ICRC has a right, under customary international law, to non-disclosure of information obtained by its employees during service. It is a privilege that is held by the organisation -- the international organisation, the ICRC. And, therefore, there being an absolute bar under customary law, the evidence of an ICRC employee is not admissible. Well, by parity of reasoning, we say that information given to Mr. Traynor by an ICRC employee, that Mr. Traynor is proffering as given to him in a discussion by the ICRC employee, is also barred. You can't go through the back door, through a hearsay means, to admit evidence that would be inadmissible directly from an ICRC employee. And on that basis, Your Honour, those are my submissions and my objections to the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also, I have a few submissions on the same topic so that you have the complete picture. The position of -- first of all, the position of the Zupljanin Defence is that we fully adopt the Stanisic Defence submission on that issue. I would like to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber that yesterday evening, Sunday, which is supposed to be -- which is supposed to be a day off for most of the people, not for the Defence, we collected in our locker extracts -- handwritten extracts from the note-book of Mr. Traynor. First of all, knowing that Mr. Traynor gave a statement -- an interview to the Prosecution 11 years ago, the question is why now we have these materials. As usual, this is a lack of diligence on the Prosecution side. It's a part of their game that they are playing all the time with us, and we have a problem here because these notes are: Number 1, just extracts; number 2, they are completely illegible. Mr. Traynor is writing even worse than I, so it's absolutely impossible to find what is going on. What I can see at the first glance is: "Stojan Zupljanin be Luka" something "chief." The date is 26th of September, 1992. With the disclosure of these materials, whether the Prosecution will rely or not, we are entering into the area where we are entitled to know what is in his note-book related to the period covered by the indictment, because we are not satisfied to see only parts of his notes. We want to have everything which is in his notes, and we want to inspect the original note-book of Mr. Traynor. That's point number 1. And later on, if certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may interrupt, Mr. Pantelic. The way you express that, that would be over-broad, wouldn't it, when you say that you would wish to have access to the entirety of his note-book? That's how it case across. You didn't mean to state it that broadly, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like -- we have, in accordance with the Rules, a right to inspect every tangible object in possession of the Prosecution, and if we think that certain parts are fabricated, we are entitled to give this material to forensic expert to -- handwritten expert to confirm or to deny our allegations. That's our right. This is our right, and we are going to exercise this right. And another point which I would like to make on that issue is that in 92 ter package, Prosecution included several articles of Mr. Traynor. Namely, these are in 92 ter packages under number 3, 6, 8, 12, 13, and 16. These articles are not on the original 65 ter list, so we object to that, and we think that these articles are inadmissible, in addition to what my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan friend. The reference of these documents are 10358.03 and then 04, 05, 06, 07, and 08. With regard to these notes of Mr. Traynor related to our client because they're illegible, I have a suggestion, a technical suggestion, that Mr. Traynor, with the assistance of the Prosecution, read out these several pages of his note-book, and then this statement will be recorded, because I suppose that he is able to read his own handwriting, and then this particular statement with regard to the contents of his notes will be transferred to the transcript so that we exactly know what is here. Maybe -- it's a speculation. Maybe Mr. Traynor says that -- said that my client is a bad guy, but maybe he said that he is a good guy. We don't know. We only know that he put something with regard to our client in his note-book, but we don't have any possibility to check what is this, after 11 years of his first contact with the Prosecution. And oddly enough, my understanding is that he is now based in Brussels, one hour with the fast train, and I really don't know why we got all these documents only on the eve of his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I start by deploring the fact that the first notification that was given to us of this submission that was going to be made by both parties was by e-mail last night at 8.15 to Mr. Hani Solana, no one else in the team, and without referring to any authorities on which Mr. O'Sullivan was going to rely, and the reality is we were unaware of the submissions he was going to make, and we haven't had a chance to research the law, all of this in a situation where the Defence knew of the difficulties that we've had in obtaining the attendance of Mr. Traynor, who is the European editor of "The Guardian," and who has limited time, and they have known because I said on no less than two occasions last week that we had to get him through on Monday and Tuesday because of the videolink. So that's the first thing. The second thing is this: The Defence have had the 92 ter package since July of last year. We can't at the moment find the Zupljanin response, and there's no reference in your judgement to it, and it may well be that they never responded at all. The Stanisic team made a response on the 31st of August, out of time, and, indeed, Your Honours, disregarded it, and no mention was made that there was going to be an objection taken on the grounds outlined today before Your Honours. Your Honours, it may be the first matter you want to consider is whether, given all of that, they're entitled to raise these various objections. But if they are, then, Your Honours, the only thing that we can do is ask Your Honours to adjourn so that we can actually have an opportunity to look at the law and to deal with the matter properly, because it's obviously a matter of importance. Your Honours, that's really -- before I go on, I can deal, off the top of my head, if I can put it that way, with the various objections that are raised, but if Your Honours are going to take this submission, as it were, into account, well, then I'm afraid we have no option - it's most regrettable - but to ask Your Honours at least to adjourn until 11.00 so we can look at the articles. But we say it's deplorable, and we could have used Friday of last week, the extra hour that this has taken at the last moment. In respect, I can deal very quickly with the 65 ter aspect, which was explained to Mr. O'Sullivan, who was going to raise it. He's accepted it. Apparently, Mr. Pantelic doesn't. We filed the package with those newspaper articles in it, saying that we were going to be advising you of the 65 ter numbers, because it was filed before the 65 ter list -- sorry, after the 65 ter list, and we were going to reply. And then you granted leave to add them to our 65 ter list, so they are on our 65 ter list. We've been through this one before. They just haven't been allocated the numbers properly. So that's a very simple one, but the rest is rather more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan. What may be a small point, Ms. Korner, by way of clarification: The notes which Mr. Pantelic says that -- the manuscript notes which Mr. Pantelic says he just had sight of overnight on the weekend, could you enlighten us as to what that's about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The notes -- Mr. Pantelic is correct in saying that the investigator who took the statement many years ago didn't ask for copies of the notes. He was -- Mr. Traynor was seen about shortly after Easter in Brussels in order to get some idea of what he had, and unfortunately he didn't have the notes with him. He then said that he would bring the notes with him when he came, and photocopies thereof. We informed the Defence of this some time ago, and they only got here yesterday. The notes were actually e-mailed to the Defence at around 5.00, both sets of Defence -- or, rather -- yes, both sets of Defence about 5.00 yesterday. I agree with Mr. Pantelic, they are largely illegible, because they are his own notes, and, of course, he can, if required, read out the passage that Mr. Pantelic is concerned about in respect of the mention of Zupljanin. That's the reason why. But at no stage, may I say, have we been ever asked -- they've known, the Defence have known that this was going to happen, that he was arriving on Sunday with those notes. As regards the request to examine the whole of his note-book, I think there would be an objection to that from Mr. Traynor. Journalists have certain protective -- protection, and, indeed, the case of Randall gives them a certain amount of protection. But that's the situation as regards to his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. O'Sullivan, you wanted to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If it could be of assistance to the Chamber in terms of timing, the Stanisic Defence has indicated three hours for cross-examination. I don't believe we'll be anywhere near using that amount of time, so it would be much, much, much shorter, abbreviated. As far as the timing of our submission, Your Honour, the final package was received on Friday, and you can see that by the 10.000-range numbers used to identify certain newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that we need to hear you on that, Mr. O'Sullivan. Well, we have noted the submissions of Mr. O'Sullivan, which have been echoed by Mr. Pantelic, and it appears to us that there are four issues which have been raised. The two legs on which Mr. O'Sullivan's basic objections stand, as we understand it, are: One, the -- you may be seated, Ms. Korner -- are, one, the question of relevance, and, two, relevance of parts of the items which comprise the 92 package of the witness who is about to be called; and, secondly, the number of these items which may fall on the ground of being inadmissible hearsay. And I use the words "inadmissible hearsay" deliberately, because the Tribunal of the -- the jurisprudence of the Tribunal draws that distinction between admissible and inadmissible hearsay. As regards the question of relevance, it appears to us that the nature of a 92 ter package is that whenever it is sought to be relied on in a new trial, there would necessarily be portions of that package, relating to earlier trials, which are not relevant to the present exercise. And whether the Defence takes the objection immediately upon being notified or at a very late stage, as occurred in this case, doesn't remove or alleviate the burden which the Trial Chamber has to only rely on such evidence as is relevant. As regards the matter of inadmissible hearsay, again, whether the objection is taken at the 11th hour or as soon as the Defence is notified that the Prosecution is relying on these matters, the Chamber, at the end of the day, bearing in mind such objections as would be taken with any witness, whether a viva voce witness or a witness called under the provisions of 92 ter, would always have to determine the admissibility of such evidence and, when admissible, how much weight should be attached to it when assessing the body of evidence as a whole. And in terms of those two legs, which we understand to be fundamental to Mr. O'Sullivan's objections, we see no reason to delay the calling of the present witness, because as I would have said, those objections remain live at all times in the course of a trial. As regards the -- what I would describe as the supplementary or ancillary objection of Mr. O'Sullivan about the derivative evidence of the witness who is about to be called, Mr. Traynor, from what would have been reported to him by an ICRC employee, of course, inasmuch as the privilege is that of the ICRC, it would, it appears to us, depend in the particular case on what the -- on what privilege is claimed, and it is something which, having regard to principles of customary law to which Mr. O'Sullivan has helpfully -- of which Mr. O'Sullivan has helpfully reminded us, be a matter to be determined in each individual case, based on the particular application. Finally, in terms of the notes to which Mr. Pantelic referred, in answer to an intervention by myself as to how broad his application was, and Mr. Pantelic did confirm that he thought he should have access to all of the notes, of course, it appears that such an over-broad application necessarily falls, and the notes which, according to Ms. Korner, she has made available, having recently come into possession of them and passed on to the Defence, the practical way of dealing with it, I would have thought, would be to -- when the witness is on the stand, to -- if, as -- I can't remember now who would have said it, the witness, himself, could be referred to the notes and could read his own handwriting, unless he's like me and can't even read his own handwriting, but that's an aside. Finally, the Chamber is not unaware of the fact that this witness is a journalist, and it means that qualitatively his evidence is a combination -- being a combination of his own observations and material gleaned from a variety of sources, because, of course, the rules about what facts are obtained and received which apply in a courtroom does not apply to the art of journalism, it means that the Chamber will at no stage lose sight of that fact. And when all is said and done, it remains a question of what weight is to be given to such of Mr. Traynor's evidence is admissible. And for those reasons, we take note of the objections raised by the Defence, but we see no reason to delay the calling of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention one more thing which has come out of this morning's activities, as it were. Could it be made clear that if counsel for the Defence are proposing to raise legal arguments and rely on authorities, that they must be obliged to give the Prosecution notice of the gist of those arguments. No notice was given of that. And, secondly, give the names and dates of the cases on which they rely. It didn't occur to me. I had to tell counsel from Canada that this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was just going to ask, do we need to say that? I would have thought the practice of the Tribunal is such that that is, as a matter of both courtesy and efficiency, something that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of your decision regarding the parts of the note-book of Mr. Traynor, how -- what is your view? Mr. Traynor will read out in the court all these pages of his note-book or he will dictate these notes to someone and then we shall have the transcript of what is exactly here? I mean, I'm perfectly fine with both options, but I would like to know, if he's going to read his note-books for the record here, that it should be at the very beginning of his testimony, because we have to know what is inside. We have to check stuff during this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know that I have a view, Mr. Pantelic. But off the top of my head, it seems to me that inasmuch as he's the Prosecution's witness, that it may be of assistance if counsel leading him were to draw his particular attention to the relevant pages so that you would then flag those pages to assist your cross-examination. That's just a thought that occurs to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but my point is the following: We need all and every word of his note-book which was disclosed to us. I don't want to rely on the choice of the Prosecution which part of this note-book we'll be examining. I'm interested in the whole part, and I cannot read his handwriting. That's the point, Your Honour. I don't want to -- and I have a right to explore everything which was disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it seems to me that the most simple way of going about this is for you to ask the witness what these notes are, because none of us know. I haven't even seen the notes yet. So the first thing we would wish to know, if we are going to go any further into this, which I don't think we need, but if you insist, then it would be for you to ask him what the notes are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. They are disclosure, which is why Your Honours haven't got a copy of them. They aren't loaded into e-court, because we rely on the statement. And we were asked to provide his notes of disclosure, but if Your Honours want to see the notes -- obviously, we say that asking him to read out every word is not a useful way. If there are certain passages that Mr. Pantelic wants to know about, of course, the witness can read them out. They're not, in fact, that bad. It takes -- it's slow, but you can actually read it. But do Your Honours want to have copies, because we can arrange that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, may I respond? In these notes, we don't know what is inside. I don't want to speculate. Again, I'm saying that. I just want, from the author of these notes, to read every particular word, because this is my role, as a Defence counsel, to explore everything which was disclosed to us. That's our role. We cannot proceed in the other way to saying, Well, Witness, what is in this part, or, What is in that part? This is a document, this is an official document. We have to know what is inside. And I propose that maybe Mr. Traynor will read out, in the Office of the Prosecution, this couple of pages, and then we should get a proper not statement but proper transcript of the contents of these notes, because once the material is disclosed, then it's over. We are entitled to know what's inside, so we don't want to have any restriction with that regard, Your Honour. How, technically, during the break or even later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the Court is not minded to ask Mr. Traynor to read out his entire note-book in a court session. I mean, this would take hours, and this is not a reasonable way of spending court time. My suggestion is that we can ask him what it is, and if that gives you grounds for wanting to explore further the contents of the notes, then I suggest that the witness is being asked to read out on a tape this afternoon the contents of his note-book, and then a copy of the tape can be given to you, or something of that kind. But for the moment, I think that the discussions about these things should be brought to an end and that we should bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree to Your Honour's -- that was exactly my proposition, technically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, how many pages are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Roughly, regarding -- the other pages are related to Visegrad and Zvornik, which are not municipalities related to my client. But as far as I see here, Banja Luka and Kotor Varos, it's around 16 pages, but not of A4 format. It's a smaller, like Hemingway's style note-book which Mr. Traynor used.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can assist with this practical issue. There are, in fact, about 10 separate note-books, small note-books, of which Mr. Traynor used during the course of 1992. He has approximately 10 of them, which he brought with him last night. When he was originally seen just after Easter, he had one note-book with him, the one which contains the Zupljanin reference, and he was asked to go back and review his other note-books, which he had in his home, to see if there were any relevant parts which were -- well, any parts which were relevant to the issues in this case. So when he arrived yesterday, he had gone through his note-books and reviewed them in their entirety, and had selected the three portions which relate to Zvornik, Visegrad, and his interview with Mr. Zupljanin, and made copies of those, and those were disclosed. If Mr. Pantelic wishes to see the note-books in their entirety, my suggestion is he sits down -- he had the opportunity to do that with Mr. Traynor in the last six weeks. He could have asked to do that previously, and there's been no request to do that. But the witness will give evidence that he has selected these portions once he was told which areas our indictment covered, and this is his selection, the portions that relate to Mr. Zupljanin, the -- yeah, the notes he made of the interview at the time, and he can be asked about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you kindly make the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Could you begin by telling us your name, your profession, and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ian Traynor. Date of birth, 11/11/55. A journalist for the newspaper "The Guardian."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you have been employed or occupied as such since when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For "The Guardian" since, let me think, 1987. And prior to that, the BBC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any regional tribunal dealing with the issues --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution. And as you would be aware, these are adversarial proceedings, in the sense that one side calls you. The other side has an opportunity to cross-examine you. The Bench may ask questions after any redirect that the side calling you has. The time allotted, it is expected that you will be giving evidence over two days, today and tomorrow. And the procedure of this Tribunal allows a certain expedited process, in the sense that a portion of the testimony on which the side calling you, in this case the Prosecution, is relying comprises documents which they would seek to have admitted. The time which they have been given is two hours for your examination-in-chief. And the counsel for each of the two accused have indicated that their cross-examination would not exceed three hours. Indeed, we have been alerted this morning that counsel for the first accused, Mr. Stanisic, are not likely to be anywhere near that time. For certain technical reasons dealing with the tapes and things of that nature, and also allowing time for the interpreters, is that the Tribunal -- is that each session is for not more than 90 minutes, after which there's a 20-minute break and we resume. And because the three courtrooms which the Tribunal has have to be shared among the several trials that are going on, the day's sitting is either from 9.00 in the morning to 1.45 in the afternoon or from 2.15 until 7.00 in the evening. We are scheduled to sit this morning and tomorrow morning. And before I invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin, I would alert you that although you have only been ushered into the courtroom, the Chamber took the bench at the usual time at 9.00. So it is 10.06 now, and the first break that we would take would be at 10.25. And before I invite Ms. Pidwell to begin, if, notwithstanding those usual times I've indicated, of course, if there is any point at which you need a break, if you indicate it to us, then we would, of course, accommodate you. Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, you've made two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, one on the 26th of March, 1999, and a second on the 9th of March in the year 2000. Have you had the opportunity to review those statements recently?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you require any changes to your 92 ter statements?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you confirm that the statements are true and correct, to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if you were asked similar questions today, would your answers be those contained in these statements?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, there are 15 newspaper articles which were written by the witness, which form part of his 92 ter package. Your Honours' ruling of the 2nd of October excluded the list of his entire articles from his period of time in the Balkans but included these 15 articles. And at this juncture, I'd like to tender his 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to put on the record that if the part of 92 ter package is the articles that I just this morning mentioned under 10358.3 and until 08, I am objecting to these particular articles to be a part of 92 package. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I had thought we had addressed this issue. I'm happy to address Your Honours again on it, if required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we propose to conditionally admit the package, and make a determination on final admission when the witness's testimony is completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it will be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Therefore, Your Honours, Exhibit numbers will be P1356.1 through P1356.17, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, you've brought some note-books into court with you. Perhaps as a preliminary step, could you please describe the note-books that you have?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: These are my note-books from 1992, when I was working in the former Yugoslavia, some of them. I mean, some of them are certainly from the period September/October 1992. And it's almost 20 years ago, and I need to feel a bit more secure, occasionally refreshing my memory, making reference to them, because it's difficult to remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are these notes that you made contemporaneously with the events that occurred in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, these are -- these are the note-books taken -- taken at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to review them over the past few weeks?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you came to The Hague yesterday, did you hand over portions of the note-books that you considered were relevant to the aspects in the case before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I handed over photocopies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, in particular, you had selected your notes from April 1992, when you visited Visegrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And also your notes from September 1992, when you conducted an interview with the accused Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And then during your proofing session, we reviewed your notes from your time in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Not directly in Zvornik; in Mali Zvornik, on the other side, on the Serbian side, yes, mmm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And those were also photocopied last night?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you some general questions about your background first. You told His Honour that you had been a correspondent with the BBC before you were employed by "The Guardian." What did you do before that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Before I worked with the BBC, I worked as a translator and interpreter, and then I worked as a monitor, also at the BBC, as a Russian graduate. And I worked as a Russian monitor with the BBC, monitoring the Soviet media at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Russian, German, reasonable French, and Croatian Serbian to a degree. I understand it, at least, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What was your level of understanding of B/C/S in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: A lot less than it is now. One would work with translators as a rule, but I would say that my knowledge was sufficient to know when I was getting an accurate translation or not. I would often have to ask for corrections or elucidations of the versions I was being given because I could tell I wasn't given a full and accurate translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And at the time you gave your second interview to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2000, you were based in Moscow. Did you go straight from Moscow to your base in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: No. I was based in Vienna from the beginning of 1989 to 1995, during which period I covered the Yugoslav wars. I first went to Belgrade in 1988, so continuously for seven years until the Dayton Conference. After that, I moved to Germany, first to Bohn and then to Berlin, and covered German politics, and then I moved to Moscow in 1999 [Realtime transcript read in error "1989"], where I was there for three years. And I'm now based in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what is your role in Brussels?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm the newspaper's Europe editor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I think this is page 25, line 15. I think witness said "1999," not "1989."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. I said 1999, I moved to Moscow from Germany in 1999. I moved to Vienna to cover Eastern Europe and the Balkans in 1989 at the beginning, January 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you can see on the transcript, Mr. Traynor, that it's a typo, Your Honour. It's Moscow in 1989, and I heard that you said "1999," so that was the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because we have to keep the transcript clear, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just to clarify, from 1989 to 1995, you were based in Vienna, covering the Balkan region?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Mmm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you explain, briefly, your modes of research and sources for the articles that you wrote over that period?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: My source of research, basically, as a reporter you're on the ground, you're travelling around different parts of the country talking to lots of people, and that's a fundamental repertorial instrument. You're reading -- listening to the local media, getting transcripts, getting translations, looking at the local newspapers, talking to officials, and talking to diplomats, talking to international people stationed in the region, and using your eyes and ears, and watching and seeing what you're seeing. That's your fundamental, as a reporter in a very kind of fast-moving, dynamic situation -- that's your basic -- your basic methodology --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were you given any specific instruction on what aspects of the conflict or incidents to cover in the region at the time by your editor or publisher?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Not really. I mean, editors leave it up to the correspondents on the ground. They're supposed to know best what's going on, and people in London, however, have an input in what might appear interesting, from that point of view, depending on what's happening elsewhere, and they would ask you to follow things up. But, by and large, you're left to your own devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you the sole correspondent for "The Guardian" at that time, or did you have others working with you?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, there was several of us. I was the main anchor correspondent since it was my beat, so to speak. However, the story was so huge at the time that, of course, we needed various people. We had someone in -- someone based in Belgrade, and we had at least two, three, four people making periodic trips from London.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you sometimes team up with other journalists from other newspapers to do research or interviews?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: More often than not, and certainly in former Yugoslavia, first in Croatian and then in Bosnia, it would be unwise to be travelling alone. One felt there would be safety in numbers, and, you would, you know -- basically the country -- you were travelling in a war zone, constantly encountering check-points and being stopped. So, you know, you would tend to travel in convoy if you were travelling, and then you would also work with colleagues. You would develop relationships with other journalists, and you would tend to work in twos or threes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you say that you followed the local news at the time. Can you comment on what kind of news was coming out generally in the beginning of 1992 in Bosnia, when you were there?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the local media was -- was a key factor in the political development, not only in Bosnia but in the former Yugoslavia as a whole. If you're following the politics of the region and you had to try and understand what was happening, it was very important, in particular, to follow the Belgrade media under Slobodan Milosevic, since the state -- the public television and the main newspapers, such as "Politika" or "Borba" were incredibly important to get an idea of what was going on. They tended to still operate in the old kind of Communist -- using the old Communist media control methods, so they're sending signals, you're getting information, you're getting lots of propaganda. Similarly, in Zagreb you also had to read the local newspapers, such as "Vjesnik," which was the main Communist Party organ before -- before the war, when the Communist administration still existed. The media were -- the local media were terribly important, also to -- to stoking trouble, causing friction, causing tension, making allegations, and basically engendering the public mood and preparing it for war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to explain, I'm going to pause in between my question and answer to allow the people who are recording this in various languages and on the monitor to catch up. Can you give us an example of the local media, as you've just referred to it, making allegations and engendering the public mood?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, regularly -- I mean, the staple diet in Belgrade television at the time under Mr. Mitrovic and Milosevic was to preach lessons about -- once the war started about Muslim fundamentalism, about Jihadism, about the green transversal, for example, which was supposed to be the kind of Islamic state that was going to be taking control all the way from Tehran straight across the Balkans to -- and Turkey and across the Balkans into Albania including Bosnia. This is the kind of thing that you would hear the whole time, prior to which you did have the kind of forthright allegations when Germany was playing quite a big role in the diplomacy surrounding the Balkan conflict. There was a lot of propaganda coming out of Belgrade on the television and newspapers about German-controlled Europe, the 4th Reich, the Ustasha, the fascist, the Vatican, the Catholic conspiracies, and so on and so on. I mean, it was nonstop.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you now about some of your articles that you wrote during the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure if you want me to assist you in this regard, but you may see that in the witness's second statement there is a list of the 170 articles that he wrote in 1992. Now, as I was reviewing them, I couldn't see any logical pattern to their order, and we have re-listed them in chronological order. I have that in hard copy, if Your Honours would like that as assistance and a guide while reviewing these. Otherwise, well, I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we are three minutes short of the break, so if that -- if you could take advantage of that to make it available to us, that would be of assistance, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In your statement, you talk about going into Visegrad, in that area, from Belgrade in 1992, and there are three articles that you've written on consecutive days in April. Did you actually go into Visegrad, itself?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: We went to the -- within the town boundaries, yes. We didn't go into the center of the town. We went -- we were with the Serbian forces -- the JNA forces at the time, and we went as far as we could in safety, but it was quite a dangerous situation. We couldn't go any farther.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what had brought you there to that region?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, it was a very hard period -- early months, April, May, June, July, it was a very hot period in the war. We were in Belgrade at the time. We were picking up lots of reports and rumours about bad things happening in Eastern Bosnia and around Zvornik and Bijeljina, places like that. We went to the border, to Mali Zvornik, on the other side of the river, where refugees were coming across, and you could speak to people and you could visit camps and hospitals and places like that. We couldn't, however, get across to the other side, so we basically headed south, still on the Serbian side of the border, and drove across into South-Eastern Bosnia, and basically by chance -- I mean, there was no particular design to this, you're just basically on a fishing expedition, in fact, to see what you would get, and we basically ran into the front-line ahead of the JNA forces that were based in that part of Serbia and were about to be crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So what did you see on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: On the Serbian side, we saw a massive military build-up. It was the Uzice Corps of the JNA, and, you know, artillery pieces, tanks, trains, trucks. There was a huge mobilisation going on being transported into that part of Bosnia, heading towards Visegrad. We were ahead of that, and basically our first encounter -- it was a very kind of strange situation, a very eerie situation. Everything was deserted. The roads were empty, nothing was moving. And in these situations, it can be quite dangerous to carry on driving because you don't know where you're heading. We drove through a tunnel which had been kind of semi-blown up and then cleared to be made passable, and we stopped at a kind of roadside cafe where we encountered a guy who described himself as the commander, and he was from Belgrade. His family was from that part of Bosnia. He basically portrayed himself -- depicted himself as a kind of fighter, kind of guerrilla fighter who is going out in the hills at night with his colleagues ahead of the main invasion force that was coming across the border. And we spent a couple of days with him ahead of the -- before the officers from the JNA kind of caught up, at which point they ordered us back.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, we were talking about your articles and your experience in relation to Visegrad before the break. And I'm wondering if I can have 65 ter 10358.03 up on the screen, please. Sir, this is one of the -- this is the first article you wrote in a series of three during your time in Visegrad, and my question is: You refer to -- you use the term "Serbian irregulars" throughout. You can see it at the beginning and also throughout the text, you use that term. And I'm asking if you could explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, these were non-JNA/Yugoslav Army fighters that were already in the region with the army forces still coming across the border. They were not -- they were uniformed. They were kind of -- they were not regular army, army folks. It was what would be described as special forces, or how they would describe themselves as special forces. The man who referred to himself as the commander, for example, told a story about having served in the French Foreign Legion in various parts of the world and had come back to fight for Serbia, had been based in Belgrade, and had come down here to represent the kind of vanguard before the kind of uniformed forces from Serbia proper came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we would go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You say, later on in your article, and it's at the top of page 2 of the English -- I think it might be the bottom of the previous page, I'm sorry, in the B/C/S, you say that: "There is little doubt that they and the Serbian irregulars are moving in for the kill," "they" meaning the army of the JNA. So you obviously formed the view in this article, and in your subsequent ones, that they were co-operating together. On what basis did you form that view?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I was with them. As they moved towards Visegrad, they were together. I was standing beside them as they were firing rockets into Visegrad, both from artillery pieces -- both Montenegrin irregulars, I would call them. There was one chap in particular who had fought in Croatia who had taken part in the -- so he said, had taken part in fighting at Cavtat in Southern Croatia and in the siege of Dubrovnik, and had come there with his colleagues to -- he was not in the Yugoslav Army, but the two -- the two different elements were side by side, and I was with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: During this time, did you see any regular police presence?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, or directly to you, Mr. Traynor, the fact that you were with these special forces, and the fact that you saw them fire artillery towards the areas that you describe, doesn't necessarily imply that there was co-operation. So could you dwell a little further on your understanding of what the co-operation was? How was it evidenced, other than the fact that they were shooting at the same target as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were using the same equipment. They were, you know, advancing along the road in formation together. They were talking to each other. They were attacking what they regard as a common enemy. There was nothing, to my eyes that I could see that suggested that they were -- they were not collaborating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you evidence any co-ordination meetings with the JNA and these special forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Conversations -- they were speaking to each other the whole time, and setting up equipment on the roadside, setting up artillery pieces, mortars. We got caught in a fire-fight. This kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 3379, please, on the screen. This is an article dated the following day, the 15th of April, 1992. Sorry, can I have the second page of this article in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And in this article, you say: "As the combined forces closed on the town, supported by heavy cannon fire, there was little sound or sign of resistance, save for the odd burst of sniper fire." Were you actually there when these combined forces closed in on the town?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say there was little sign of resistance, could you expand on that, please?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't -- I mean, we were witnessing a kind of deafening, you know, artillery assault on the town. Apart from the odd burst of sniper fire -- as I wrote here, we got caught in a fire-fight. It's kind of heavily wooded territory on either side of the road, and there were people shooting out of the forest. Apart from that, there was no return of fire from the cannon fire, the mortars, the 120-millimetre pieces that were firing into Visegrad. We couldn't determine any return of fire whatsoever, apart from the odd burst of machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if I could have the next article, please. It's 65 ter 3378.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: This is the article you wrote on your last day in Visegrad on the 16th of April, where you talk about the attack having happened on the Tuesday evening. This is a Thursday. And you use the term -- perhaps I should wait for the article to come up. It's in the second paragraph in the English, you use the term "mopping-up of the last pockets of Muslim resistance." Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what you mean by that turn of phrase?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, that's what the so-called irregulars would describe they were doing. I mean, the place was empty, it was deserted. People had fled. They'd fled very quickly. They'd left everything -- you know, you could -- if you'd been around the former Yugoslavia for a long time, you'd seen this thing so many times before, and villages had just been very quickly abandoned, with the washing still on the line, animals running, you know, wandering around, et cetera, and no people, but the irregulars would -- would set off to -- what they would describe as to clear out the last remaining locals, Muslims in this case, and there was clearly still small-scale attacks and fire going on that you could hear and see. But apart from that, the place had basically been abandoned very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And later on in that article, you talk about witnessing an interview with this Colonel Jankovic -- Jovanovic, and you witness him being interviewed by a journalist from the Belgrade newspaper "Politika," and you call it a mouthpiece for Slobodan Milosevic. How did you form that opinion? Why did you make that comment?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, "Politika," had long -- you know, since long before in the late 1980s Milosevic took over the Serbia media, installed his own editors and staff at the newspaper, the most important newspaper in Belgrade, and in this particular instance you could see the journalist from Belgrade basically briefing, what we would -- in modern politics, what we call spin-doctoring, briefing the general in what he should be saying to international journalists, which indicated to me the kind of -- the influence that the main regime newspapers and broadcasters in Belgrade could play. I mean, the report about -- the Serbian journalist clearly felt himself in a position to instruct a federal army officer on what was the best thing to say to people like me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your statement lists the 170 articles that you wrote in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And I think Your Honours have received the chronological order of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And we can see from that that you didn't write any articles from the 31st of July, 1992, until the 22nd of August, 1992. Does that sound correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: The first day, it was the 31st of July? Yeah, I went on holiday, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And before you went on holiday, where were you -- do you recall where you were based or what you were reporting about?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I would need to consult the articles, but, I mean, fundamentally somewhere in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first heard about the existence of any detention camps in Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Basically, the story of the camps, for the international reportings, the stories and the rumours and speculations started emerging, I'd say, roughly in the second half of July, around this period that you're referring to. It was secondary, it was uncorroborated. There were no -- there was no real international presence in North-West Bosnia at the time. It was on the basis of refugees and witness stories coming out. But as a basis for, you know, writing a proper hard newspaper article, to my mind, it was insufficient, and I also would like to think it wouldn't have got past the editors in London, it just wouldn't have cut the mustard. There were, however, other newspapers that were beginning to write about this kind of thing. Notably I recall I think Gutman, from "Newsday," the American journalist, was already writing stories about reports, rumours, et cetera. So there was -- you know, there was a lot of interest, and it's a fairly competitive business, so there were people trying to get into the region. What happened, I went on holiday. I think there was a London conference in early August where Radovan Karadzic and various Yugoslav political leaders attended the London Conference under John Major. I attended that also and then took some time off, a couple of weeks. All these stories were beginning to surface, and Karadzic was challenged in London by international journalists on the existence or non-existence of these so-called concentration camps. And, of course, he was denying categorically that any such thing existed, at which point he was challenged by a colleague of mine from "The Guardian" and ITN British Television News, to be taken there to inspect, and that's basically what happened. Karadzic -- they flew to Belgrade. Karadzic flew them up to Banja Luka and Prijedor, and they went to some of these camps. And, of course, it was fairly dramatic, particularly, television footage that went around the world and caused an international, you know -- bit of a crisis, really, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 2329. This is a video of the ITN footage from this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we ask what the nexus is between this video and the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, he's just testified about his knowledge of what was happening within the media towards the end of July and August. It's fully accepted this is not his product, but this is the footage that was aired and was based on the information that was reported at the time by these reporters. Now, we have -- this is ITN footage. We have two ITN footage. We have one ABC "Night-line" video and another ITN documentary, which we're going to ask this witness as the only journalist that you're going to hear from to comment on and tender these items through. In a perfect world, we would have called every single journalist or cameraman who did this footage, but we don't have that privilege in this trial. So we are asking that we can tender the media footage that we have through the only witness who is a member of the media at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Precisely the point, Your Honour. There's absolutely no connection between this witness and other media footage. It was open to the Prosecution to call the people who produced it, who were there. There's absolutely -- to ask him to comment on something that anyone can watch has absolutely no probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless, Mr. O'Sullivan, of course, the -- a precisely-phrased question is whether what we could all observe, in which we include the witness, is something that he can independently -- or correspondingly, for want of a better word, testify to. Do you follow what I'm saying? And in terms of the nexus, as I understand his testimony, he made certain observations as part of his work as a journalist. Other journalists, other persons in that craft, are following up on that, including the agencies with which he's not connected, admittedly, who would have shot this video footage, and it remains to be seen whether, in addition to the Chamber and the parties seeing the footage, whether there is any admissible question which the witness can be asked based on his own observations. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. I would kindly ask Ms. Pidwell just to give us the reference of the author of this -- actually, the name of the journalist, if it's available, of this video footage, and precisely the date when it was made, yeah, for the record just.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The authors, and they'll introduce themselves, are Penny Marshal and Ian Williams. The date is August, and we can pull up the exact date in a moment. I'm told we need to go to Sanction to actually play the video. The date is either the 5th or 6th of August, but we'll just confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: "The Bosnian Serbs don't call Omarska a concentration camp. Come in, they challenged ITN, and see it for yourselves. Under Serbian armed guard for our own protection, a three-day journey ended here at the gates of a disused mine in Northern Bosnia. Here we were shown only several hundred of the two and a half thousand prisoners, all Muslim men at Omarska, we were told, to be interrogated. Those found guilty of fighting Serbs were then sent to prisoner of war camps, the innocent to refugee camps. This is all we saw of the prisoners and of Omarska itself. They never spoke. The only voices, those of the guards ordering them to eat faster and leave. How are you treated, what are the conditions, I asked. "I don't want to tell lies. I can't speak the truth. Thank you for coming. "We were told that the army does not control Omarska, that these prisoners are the responsibility of the civil authorities and local militia. We sought an explanation from the camp commandant. "Would you describe this as a prison camp, a transit camp, or a refugee camp? "No, this is not a camp. This is a centre, a transit centre. Omarska and Trnopolje both, they're centres, not camps. "And then the men left back to wherever they'd come from away from our cameras and questions, hidden from the United Nations and the Red Cross who've been denied access to Omarska, hidden until now from the world. We were not allowed to follow them to their living accommodation, in what appeared to be the larger of the two buildings, to see the other 2.000 detainees and how they live. What's your reason? "Just to try to, to do my best here. "What's your reason to -- not to show us where they live? "When Dr. Karadzic -- "Oh, well. "Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "He promised us something else and said you can do this and this and that and not that. "We seen nothing, we seen one dining hall and 80 prisoners. And so we left, our host fulfilling their promise to show us the second camp, Trnopolje where 2.000 refugees are living. We were not prepared for what we saw and heard there. How long has he been here? Several hundreds said that they'd arrived from Omarska that morning or from another detention camp, released to this refugee centre after days, sometimes months of interrogation. We asked if the allegations of beating in the detention centres were true. "I can say much about that. Some people [indiscernible]. "I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that, you know. I -- can you understand me? "Tell us the truth. "[B/C/S spoken]. "Killed? What happened? In this vicious civil war, where atrocities against Serbs as well as Muslims occur daily, finding the truth isn't easy. We ourselves saw no evidence of beatings on any refugee here, and we only heard the allegations, allegations even the camp doctor seemed unable to substantiate in front of our Serb hosts. Does he get any cases here of people who've been beaten from the other camps? "Yes. "Many? "Yes. " Would you be happier speaking another language? "I was able, however, to smuggle out a role of film, and a man who took these pictures and gave it to me said he would be killed if caught. He begged me to check that in three days he was still alive. And amongst all this horror, some small touches of humanity. "This is my friend. "Like 19-year-old Igor, a Serb, who now stands guard over the fence he grew up with. Muslims from the village they once shared as children, now homeless, persecuted, and behind wire. Igor took us to another side of Trnopolje, where we met some who'd come here by choice, those who'd run for their lives to this pitiable camp. Amongst them, 13-year-old Sana who said he was used as a human shield by extremist Muslims on his own side. The Serbs had taken his mother. Are you frightened now? "Yes, a little. "Where do you want to be? If you could shut your eyes and be anywhere, where would you like to be? "To follow my mother, to find my mother. Where is she? "No one we spoke to knew why they'd been brought here, whether they were prisoners, refugees, or what lay in store for them. In this civil war, there is no sense and a great deal of horrifying cruelty. "Penny Marshal, News at 10, Northern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, did you ever visit Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you visit Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Also September -- I think twice in September and October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the footage that you saw in that report of Trnopolje, is that an accurate account of what you also personally saw?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, it was different. It was changing rapidly in those days. By the time I was there -- what you see here is mostly young males. By the time I was there, they had all been shipped out, mostly, either to the south or to the north, but there was still, you know, a couple thousand people there when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the setup of the camp there, had it -- was it the same when you saw it or had it changed in some way?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: There wasn't the same wire in -- you know, confined -- confinement behind wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the people who were guarding the facility at the time that you went in September, who were they, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, they were -- they were local either military or police forces, and also the Serbian Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you at some stage interview people who had been -- who said that they had been detained in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed, yeah. I mean, a lot of these people were evacuated in convoys in October 1992. I spoke to dozens of people who were in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did you conduct those interviews?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: In Karlovac, in Croatia. They were taken out in convoys to -- former army barracks in Croatia, outside of Zagreb and confined there before being scattered across Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances of the interviews? Did you -- can you describe how they came about and the procedure that you underwent when interviewing these people?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: It was -- basically, in Croatia it was a refugee emergency, and a scandal of the camps had been unearthed by this kind of television coverage had brought a lot of international pressure for the camps to be closed down. They were closed down rather quickly. There had been endless convoys through that summer of people from that region being shipped down south into Travnik on the other side of the front-line. Thousands of people had gone in that direction. And then the Croats were claiming it was a bit of an emergency, and they closed the border to the north. So it was kind of a pressure-cooker effect. There was nowhere to go. But then there were these convoys, busloads of these people taken to Karlovac, purely on the condition that they would be kept there until other European or other -- they could go elsewhere in Europe. They wouldn't be allowed to stay in Croatia. So they were there for weeks, and I spent a long time, probably up to a fortnight, every day just going back and forth there and conducting, you know, very lengthy interviews with many of them and just getting their stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And was there anyone -- any person in the footage that you just saw that you have subsequently met and interviewed?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Not directly, that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that as an exhibit at this junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. This witness had never been to Omarska. He said he visited Trnopolje in October 1992. This footage is from, apparently, August 1992. He gave his evidence about Trnopolje in October. He gave his evidence about Karlovac in Croatia in October. In our submission, there's no nexus between this video-clip and this witness, and, therefore, it's not admissible through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The video may be admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1357, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can have the next video, please, which is 65 ter 2817. This is the second report from ITN, Penny Marshal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we proceed, having regard to the objection which was raised to the admission of the last exhibit, the reasons for its admissibility, in the Chamber's view, is that although, as Mr. O'Sullivan has correctly said, it is not the work product of the witness on the stand, and it deals with -- although there is an overlap in terms of the camp that he did visit, that was later than the period shown in the video, we consider it admissible on its own on the basis that having regard to the sequence of events to which the witness has testified, this video had been made as a part of the process of journalists visiting the camps in question, and, to that extent, is of assistance to the Tribunal in its final determination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I apologise. I just read out the wrong 65 ter number. If we could have 65 ter 1571, which is the follow-up ITN report and has the same reporters in it. It's in Sanction, and I'm afraid we don't have a transcript of the entire portion that will be played.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: "Reporter: Inside the camp hospital, the doctor who last week stood petrified was now welcoming, the relief obvious. He now knows there's international concern for him and people like him. He says much more needs to be done, but the conditions have improved. "The families, they can come now and visit them. It's much, much better. "And the men responsible for running this camp and the others admit mistakes were made. "[B/C/S spoken]. "Some people, they lose control, and then they -- they beat people at young people and -- "But our Serbian hosts, who still control the limited access we have to the camps, were anxious to stress that equivalent atrocities have been inflicted on their own side. This video, they said, showed some of the 6.000 Serb civilians killed by Muslims, and they deny they're using terror to force Muslims from their villages, but there is evidence that they are. Kozarac, for example, was once a village of 26.000. Now there's no one left. "Many are in these camps, men like 26-year-old Senad Hukanovic, held up by his brother. He was a television repairman before the Serbs took him. "No, no fighting. " You've been in prison in Omarska for [indiscernible]? "[B/S/C spoken]. "Did you think you were going to die when you're inside? "[B/C/S spoken]. "The International Red Cross yesterday gave out registration forms to the 2.000 now in Trnopolje, a small start in one camp. There are hundreds of others they need to reach. Poor civilians on all sides because of their ethnic backgrounds have been killed in this war. These camps are only for some of the survivors. "Penny Marshal, ITN, in Northern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, that footage was taken, I think we heard the reporter say, a week later of Trnopolje. What you saw there, was that closer to what you saw at the time you visited?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You could see the place had been changed, that they'd taken down the wiring and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And there was some footage there of the journalist inside a room watching a television programme. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly where it was, but it does recall an office in Banja Luka, where they would -- where the security chief -- the police chief and his aides would show similar videos of alleged atrocities against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the footage that you saw, which said it was on the road to Kozarac, are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: I saw similar -- I drove that road and I saw similar -- very similar scenes. And Kozarac lies on the road between Banja Luka and Prijedor, and it had been, you know, comprehensively pretty much, you know, blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender that video at this stage, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. O'Sullivan, that there is the same objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, there is at least comment about his experience of having seen Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Later, in September 1992, you went to Banja Luka, when Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen came to visit and there was a meeting with Radovan Karadzic. Had you been to Banja Luka before that time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you recall from which direction you came from and how you came to Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR
